about: Shorts waiting to be posted, oldest first. To add one: put the .mp4 in site/media/shorts/ and add an entry here. The publisher posts the first entry not yet in posted.json. Optional "comment": posted as the first comment on each platform.

items.title: Your car payment could cost you $78,000
items.caption:
$1,000 a month for 5 years is $60,000 in car payments.
Invested instead at around 10% a year, the same money could have grown to about $78,000.
The car loses value. The investment can grow. (Returns are not guaranteed.)
items.comment: Would you still buy the car, or invest the payment instead? 👇

items.title: Start investing at 20 or 30? The gap is $298,066
items.caption:
$100 a month at 8% a year, invested until 65.
Start at 20: about $527,454. Start at 30: about $229,388.
Ten extra years of saving, just $12,000 more put in, is worth roughly $298,000.
items.comment: How old were you when you started investing? 👇

items.title: Your bank pays you 0.5% and charges you 20%
items.caption:
A traditional savings account can pay as little as 0.5% a year.
The same bank's credit card can charge 20% or more.
That gap is how banks make money from you.
items.comment: What interest does your savings account pay right now? 👇

items.title: When bread cost 200 billion marks
items.caption:
Germany, 1923. Prices doubled again and again until one loaf of bread cost about 200 billion marks.
This is what hyperinflation looks like.
items.comment: Could hyperinflation happen again today? Yes or no 👇

items.title: Your $5 coffee could be worth $226,659
items.caption:
$5 a day is $1,825 a year.
Invested instead for 30 years at 8% a year, compounded monthly, it grows to about $226,659.
Small habits, big numbers.
items.comment: Coffee or compounding: which one are you keeping? ☕👇

items.title: The worst deal in history?
items.caption:
In 1626, Manhattan was traded for goods worth about $24.
Invested at 6% a year for 400 years, that would be around $300 billion. At 8%, about $560 trillion, more than the whole world economy.
The returns are hypothetical, for illustration.
items.comment: Worst deal ever, or not? Tell us what you think 👇

items.title: The $5,000 debt that lasts 20 years
items.caption:
$5,000 on a card at 24% APR, paying only the minimum (interest plus 1% of the balance, $25 floor).
It takes about 19.5 years to clear, and you pay back nearly $14,000.
Pay more than the minimum, every month. Terms vary by card.
items.comment: Minimum payment or pay it off in full: what do you do? 👇

items.title: Buffett's secret nobody talks about
items.caption:
According to Morgan Housel's The Psychology of Money, $81.5 billion of Warren Buffett's $84.5 billion fortune came after his 65th birthday.
He wasn't just a great investor. He was a great investor for 70 years.
items.comment: Did you know most of his wealth came after 65? 👇

May 22 is now Bitcoin Pizza Day.

Day 20: $5,243

That's compounding. The last days do most of the work.

items.title: The 100 trillion dollar banknote
items.caption:
In 2009, Zimbabwe printed a 100 trillion dollar note.
In late 2008, prices were doubling about every day.
Within months, the country stopped using its own currency.
items.comment: Could this happen to any currency? 👇
sources: Steve Hanke & Nicholas Krus, World Hyperinflations (Cato Institute, 2012)
Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, 2009

items.title: Kodak invented the digital camera, then went bankrupt | Money Stories #1
items.caption:
In 1975, a Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson built the first digital camera.
Kodak made most of its money selling film. Digital threatened all of it.
So it moved slowly. Rivals didn't.
In 2012, Kodak filed for bankruptcy.
items.comment: Can you name a company making the same mistake today? 👇 Part 2 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: Kodak bankruptcy filing, January 2012 (Reuters, BBC)
Steve Sasson / Kodak digital camera history (Kodak, IEEE)

items.title: He tried to buy a fighter jet with Pepsi points | Money Stories #2
items.caption:
In 1996, a Pepsi ad showed a Harrier jet for seven million Pepsi points.
Pepsi let you buy extra points for ten cents each.
A student, John Leonard, raised about seven hundred thousand dollars and sent a cheque.
Pepsi refused. A court ruled the ad was a joke, not an offer.
items.comment: Would you have tried it? 👇 Part 3 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: Leonard v. PepsiCo, Inc., 88 F. Supp. 2d 116 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)

items.title: Isaac Newton lost a fortune in a stock bubble | Money Stories #3
items.caption:
In 1720, everyone in London wanted shares of the South Sea Company.
Isaac Newton bought in, sold for a profit, then watched the price keep climbing.
Then the bubble burst. Newton reportedly lost around twenty thousand pounds.
He is said to have written: I can calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.
items.comment: Have you ever bought because everyone else was? 👇 Part 4 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: Andrew Odlyzko, 'Newton's financial misadventures in the South Sea Bubble' (Royal Society, 2019)

items.title: Nobel prize winners ran a fund that nearly broke Wall Street | Money Stories #4
items.caption:
Long-Term Capital Management had two Nobel prize winning economists.
It borrowed heavily to make tiny bets look huge.
When Russia defaulted in 1998, the bets went wrong. It lost about four point six billion dollars in months.
Banks put in three point six billion dollars, in a rescue organised by the Federal Reserve, to stop the damage spreading.
items.comment: Would you trust a genius with your money? 👇 Part 5 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: Federal Reserve History: 'Near Failure of Long-Term Capital Management'

items.title: 3 money mistakes in your 20s that cost the most
items.caption:
Mistake one. Waiting to invest. Time is the biggest ingredient, and your twenties have the most of it.
One hundred dollars a month in the S&P 500 since 2006 is now worth about $95,539.
Mistake two. Paying only the minimum on a credit card. Interest keeps growing on what you still owe.
Mistake three. Every raise turns into new spending, so savings never grow.
items.comment: Which one are you guilty of? 👇
sources: S&P 500 ETF (SPY) price history, Yahoo Finance, at render time (price only, no dividends)

items.title: One joke wiped out £500 million | Money Stories #5
items.caption:
In 1991, jewellery boss Gerald Ratner gave a speech to business leaders.
He joked that some of his own products were total crap.
Customers stopped coming. About five hundred million pounds was wiped off the company's value.
Ratner lost his job. The company even changed its name.
items.comment: What's the worst business mistake you've seen? 👇 Part 6 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: BBC News: 'Gerald Ratner: the speech that cost £500m'

items.title: Compound interest explained in 20 seconds | Compound Interest #1
items.caption:
You earn interest on your money. Next year, you earn interest on that interest too.
At ten percent a year, one thousand dollars becomes about two thousand five hundred in ten years.
In thirty years, it's about seventeen thousand four hundred. Same thousand dollars. Just more time.
items.comment: Part 2: the rule of 72. Follow so you don't miss it 👇
sources: Arithmetic: 1000 × 1.1^10 = 2,594; 1000 × 1.1^30 = 17,449 (illustrative rate, not a promised return)

items.title: He threw away a hard drive with 8,000 bitcoin | Money Stories #6
items.caption:
In 2013, James Howells, in Wales, threw out an old hard drive.
He says it held about eight thousand bitcoin he mined years earlier.
It went to a landfill. The city council has refused to let him dig it up.
At today's prices those coins would be worth about $646 million.
items.comment: Would you keep digging? 👇 Part 7 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: BBC News reports on James Howells and Newport City Council (2013–2025)
Bitcoin price: Yahoo Finance, at render time

items.title: How to invest in the S&P 500 (beginner, 30 seconds)
items.caption:
The S&P 500 is a list of about five hundred of the biggest companies in America.
You can't buy the index itself. People buy an index fund or ETF that copies it, in one purchase.
One thousand dollars in an S&P 500 fund in 2010 is now worth about $6,710.
Look for low fees, invest regularly, and hold for years.
items.comment: Do you own an S&P 500 fund? 👇
sources: S&P Dow Jones Indices (index definition)
S&P 500 ETF (SPY) price history, Yahoo Finance, at render time (price only, no dividends)

items.title: A janitor quietly left $8 million | Money Stories #7
items.caption:
Ronald Read worked at a gas station and as a janitor in Vermont.
He lived simply and bought shares of solid companies, then held them for decades.
When he died in 2014, his estate was worth about eight million dollars.
He left about six million to his local library and hospital.
items.comment: Could you live this simply? 👇 Part 8 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: The Wall Street Journal and Brattleboro Reformer reports on Ronald Read's estate (2015)

items.title: The rule of 72: how fast your money doubles | Compound Interest #2
items.caption:
Divide seventy-two by your yearly return. That's roughly how many years it takes to double.
At six percent, about twelve years. At nine percent, about eight. At twelve percent, about six.
It works backwards too. Inflation at three percent halves your cash's value in about twenty-four years.
items.comment: Part 3: why starting early beats starting big 👇
sources: Rule of 72 (standard approximation for doubling time)

items.title: A secretary secretly built $9 million | Money Stories #8
items.caption:
Sylvia Bloom worked as a legal secretary in New York for sixty-seven years.
When her bosses bought stocks, she quietly bought the same ones, in smaller amounts.
She died in 2016 with more than nine million dollars.
She left over six million to a charity that helps poor students go to college.
items.comment: What would you do with $9 million? 👇 Part 9 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: The New York Times, 'A Secretary Amassed $9 Million. Then She Gave It Away.' (2018)

items.title: Start at 25 or 35? The 10-year gap | Compound Interest #3
items.caption:
Two friends invest one hundred dollars a month at eight percent a year until sixty-five.
The one who starts at twenty-five ends with about three hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
The one who starts at thirty-five ends with about one hundred and fifty thousand.
items.comment: How old were you when you started? 👇
sources: Arithmetic: future value of $100/month at 8%/yr compounded monthly (illustrative rate, not a promised return)

items.title: This company went from IPO to closed in 268 days | Money Stories #9
items.caption:
Pets dot com sold pet food online and had a famous sock puppet mascot.
It went public in February 2000, at the peak of the dot-com boom.
It sold heavy bags of food below cost and paid for shipping.
Two hundred and sixty-eight days after the IPO, it shut down.
items.comment: Which company today reminds you of this? 👇 Part 10 tomorrow, follow so you don't miss it.
sources: CNET / Wall Street Journal reports on Pets.com (2000)

items.title: 3 money mistakes in your 30s that are hard to undo
items.caption:
Mistake one. No emergency fund. One surprise bill becomes debt.
Mistake two. Buying the biggest house the bank will lend you, then having nothing left to invest.
Mistake three. No insurance while people depend on you.
items.comment: What would you add to this list? 👇
sources: General personal-finance guidance (emergency fund of 3-6 months of expenses is a widely used rule of thumb)

items.title: A 158-year-old bank collapsed in one weekend | Money Stories #10
items.caption:
Lehman Brothers was founded in 1850 and became a Wall Street giant.
It borrowed heavily and bet on mortgages. When house prices fell, the losses piled up.
On the fifteenth of September, 2008, it filed for bankruptcy, with about six hundred billion dollars in assets.
Markets around the world crashed in the weeks after.
items.comment: Where were you in 2008? 👇
sources: U.S. Bankruptcy Court SDNY filing, 15 September 2008
Federal Reserve History: 'The Great Recession and Its Aftermath'

items.caption:
Mistake one. Thinking it's too late to start. Even twenty years of steady investing can grow a lot.
For example, one thousand dollars in the S&P 500 in 2006 is now worth about $6,004.
Mistake two. Paying for everyone else's goals before your own retirement.
Mistake three. Not knowing where your money goes each month.

items.title: The one-second trick that tells you when your money doubles
items.caption:

Savings at 2%: about 36 years. Bonds at 6%: about 12 years. Stocks at an assumed 10%: about 7 years.
Same money, totally different futures.

items.title: How to split every paycheck (the 50/30/20 rule)
items.caption:
Fifty percent goes to needs. Rent, food, bills.
Thirty percent goes to wants. Eating out, trips, fun.
Twenty percent goes to your future. Savings, investing, paying off debt.
items.comment: What percentage do you actually save? 👇
sources: 50/30/20 budgeting rule (popularised by Elizabeth Warren, All Your Worth, 2005)

items.title: How much a day blows $10,000 a year?
items.caption:
Just twenty-seven dollars and forty cents a day.
Coffee, lunch, a ride, a snack. It adds up without you noticing.
That's ten thousand dollars a year. In ten years, a hundred thousand.
items.comment: What's your biggest daily spend? 👇

items.title: 3 reasons you never have enough money
items.caption:
Reason one. You save what's left after spending, and nothing is ever left. Save first, on payday.
Reason two. Small subscriptions you forgot about keep charging every month.
Reason three. Interest on debt eats your income before you see it.
items.comment: Which one is you? 👇
